findings.title: Findings converge on occurrence-side owner resolution
findings.why_it_matters: Summary step 3 finds an occurrence's owner by reusing `analysis.statement_owner_for_line`. That function was built to attach a comment token to a statement, and three of its properties cause trouble when it gets an occurrence instead. It keys a decorated `def`/`class` on the undecorated `def` line. It indexes `source.lines[line - 1]` without a bounds check. It picks containment or line equality from a 0-based comment column. Findings 2, 3, and 4 each hit one of those properties and each proposes its own local fix: a decorated-start rule, a bounds check plus a placement rule, and a new containment entry point. Is reusing comment-owner lookup for occurrences the right mechanism at all? Or should the matching rule be re-evaluated as a whole? That includes whether an occurrence needs an owner statement, and which failure modes are worth handling versus documenting as limits.
findings.recommended: A: Re-evaluate occurrence owner resolution before addressing Findings 2-4 individually
findings.chosen: A: Re-evaluate occurrence owner resolution before addressing Findings 2-4 individually

findings.title: Occurrence ownership misses decorated definitions and lets an enclosing `def`/`class` pragma claim occurrences in its body
findings.why_it_matters: `statement_key` starts a decorated `def`/`class` span at the `def` line, not the decorator. At module level, an occurrence that starts at `@decorator` has no covering statement, so only `ignore-file` can suppress it. The file phase still accepts an `ignore-next` above the decorator: placement uses the decorated start, and the pragma resolves to the `def`'s key. That pragma then matches nothing, and the user gets no signal. There's no HSL900, because the file phase accepted it, and no unused verdict (spec 010 D9). Inside a class, the same occurrence's innermost covering statement is the class itself. So `class Foo:  # house-lint: ignore[HSL104] - ...` claims it, along with any other occurrence starting on a decorator or non-statement line in that body. That is the containment the Must-hold list forbids, reached through the equality rule. The file phase's `NO_OWNER` window for `ignore-next` (`_owns`) isn't carried over either. Parent D15 makes decorators owner nodes for TypeScript, so the two languages would disagree.
findings.recommended: A: Resolve occurrences on the decorated start
findings.chosen: Superseded by Finding 1

findings.title: An occurrence line past the retained text crashes resolution, and where the step sits relative to the per-rule `try` is unstated
findings.why_it_matters: `validate_location` checks only that coordinates are positive. `statement_owner_for_line` indexes `source.lines[line - 1]`, so a line past the end of the retained text raises `IndexError`. Parent 005 D9 chose to run jscpd on real paths and ratified a known limitation: a mid-run edit, or a line-model difference (bare `\r`, form feed, BOM), "shows up as a visible finding, not a silent wrong result". A truncated file instead crashes the step. Step 2 parses each file once across rules, which puts resolution after the per-rule loop and outside the `try` at pipeline.py:346-367. The exception then escapes `run_project_phase` to the CLI boundary, and the whole run reports one internal error and no findings. If resolution ran inside the `try` instead, the generic handler would `break` and skip every later project rule.
findings.recommended: A: Treat an occurrence whose line exceeds the parsed file's line count as having no owner, so only `ignore-file` can suppress it and the finding stays visible
findings.chosen: Superseded by Finding 1

findings.title: Step 3's "trailing-comment branch" can't be selected through `statement_owner_for_line`'s API
findings.why_it_matters: The function picks its branch from `source.lines[line - 1][:column]`, using a 0-based comment-token column. Occurrence columns are 1-based and have nothing to do with a comment. For an indented occurrence at its first column, the slice is whitespace, so the standalone branch runs. That branch matches only statements that start or end on the line, so a start on a continuation line of a multi-line statement gets `None`. A top-level line at column 1 has a non-empty slice and takes the containment branch. The owner ends up depending on indentation and column units, not on a rule. To follow the ledger, the build would have to refactor the function or pass a fake column.
findings.recommended: A: Extract the containment lookup, with the except-clause refinement, into its own function that takes only a line
findings.chosen: Superseded by Finding 1

findings.title: The project phase's use of the shared pragma walk is unstated: its diagnostic sink, its enabled-rule set, and the project-rule branch
findings.why_it_matters: "New homes" says the project-phase function shares `_collect_claims`'s walk. That walk reports HSL900 through an `add_diagnostic` callback as a side effect. It takes an `enabled_rules` set, and today it skips claims for project rules (`is_project_rule` → `continue`). The ledger doesn't say three things:
findings.recommended: B: Split the walk into a pure function returning the accepted pragmas and the diagnostics
findings.chosen: B: Split the walk into a pure function returning the accepted pragmas and the diagnostics

findings.title: `group_id` has no consumer that `related` doesn't already serve
findings.why_it_matters: Audience assumption: a second consumer (#52 or CI summaries) that does not exist yet. Parent D12 justified the group id by #52 and CI summaries. Parent D16 then gave #52 its own per-occurrence identity and called the group id "separate from identity" and "unstable across runs", so #52 isn't its consumer. No CI summary exists. A finding's own location plus its `related` list already identifies its cluster. D3-A puts the key on every finding and in the cached payload, gives a single-location candidate an id that groups nothing, and needs numbering rules (Finding 9).
findings.recommended: B: Ship `related` only, and add a group id when a consumer needs it
findings.chosen: B: Ship `related` only, and add a group id when a consumer needs it

findings.title: The `related` entry type adds a third location shape
findings.why_it_matters: "New homes" adds a public location type in results.py for `related` entries. Two location shapes already exist: `project_rule.Location`, which holds a `LoadedFile`, and `Finding`'s four flat coordinate fields. The critic proposes one `Span` shared by `Finding`, `related`, and `ProjectCandidate`. Only part of that holds:
findings.recommended: A: Keep the design
findings.chosen: A: Keep the design

findings.title: Large clusters: quadratic `related`, no project candidate budget, and per-occurrence linear scans
findings.why_it_matters: Audience assumption: a repo large enough that a duplicate rule reports thousands of locations on first enabling. Each of n occurrences lists its n-1 siblings, so a 500-copy cluster produces about 250k `related` entries in JSON. Text output (D4) prints 499 locations on each of 500 lines. `statement_owner_for_line` scans every statement for each occurrence (O(k·S) per file). File rules are bounded by `MAX_CANDIDATES_PER_FILE`, while the ledger explicitly leaves project rules without a budget.
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation
findings.chosen: B: Accept as a known limitation

findings.title: Group-id numbering when a rule fails or a candidate is fully suppressed is unspecified
findings.why_it_matters: If the id counter advances inside the comprehension at pipeline.py:347-359, a rule that fails partway uses up ids that no finding carries, and later rules' ids shift. The ledger also doesn't say whether a fully suppressed candidate uses up an id. The effect is gaps, or shifted ids between runs whose outcomes already differ. D3 documents ids as unstable across runs, and they're only compared for equality within one run, so no consumer contract breaks.
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation
findings.chosen: Moot: Finding 6 dropped group_id

findings.title: A project-phase parse failure is assumed to have been reported by the file phase
findings.why_it_matters: Step 2 doesn't re-report a file that fails to parse in the project phase, on the grounds that the file phase already reported it. That holds today:
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation
findings.chosen: B: Accept as a known limitation

findings.title: Findings converge on the project phase re-deriving the file phase's pragma-acceptance verdict
findings.why_it_matters: The ledger states that "a pragma is accepted in one phase exactly when it is accepted in the other". Nothing enforces it. `project_suppressions` doesn't receive the file phase's verdict. It re-runs `scan_pragmas(source, (rule_id,))` and relies on two outside facts: each location's file is one of the rule's retained inputs, and acceptance depends on the enabled set only through the disabled-rule check. Three critics reached this from different directions. Senior-engineer found that nothing checks a `Location`'s file against the rule's input (Finding 2). Contract-caller found that the `(rule_id,)` substitution is unpinned (Finding 3). Structural-minimalist found that no test crosses per-file-ignores with a project-rule pragma (folded into Finding 3). Each proposes its own guard or test. Should the re-derivation be re-evaluated as a mechanism, instead of guarding each assumption it rests on? That includes whether the drift is worth handling at all, or should be documented as a limitation.
findings.recommended: B: Keep the re-derivation and address Findings 2 and 3 individually.
findings.chosen: B: Keep the re-derivation and address Findings 2 and 3 individually.

findings.title: Pragma acceptance assumes a location's file is in the rule's input, and nothing checks it
findings.why_it_matters: `project_suppressions` treats `(rule_id,)` as the enabled set because "a file is in rule R's input only if R applies to it". `visible_occurrences` never checks that `occurrence.location.file` is one of the files passed to `rule.run`, and `Location.file` can be any `LoadedFile`. Suppose a rule builds its own `LoadedFile` or reports a file that per-file-ignores removed from its input. The project phase then honours a pragma that the file phase reported as "unused suppression for disabled rule". The existing test `test_a_rule_can_only_report_on_files_it_was_given` (test_project_phase.py:492) holds only because the stand-in `Recorder` reports on the files it gets. It doesn't test any engine check. (The critic's further claim, that this breaks the "read exactly once" invariant, overstates things. That invariant protects cached file-phase results, and the project phase is uncached. The pragma mismatch stands without it.)
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation: a project rule that reports a location in a file outside its input bypasses the per-file-ignores parity, silently.
findings.chosen: B: Accept as a known limitation: a project rule that reports a location in a file outside its input bypasses the per-file-ignores parity, silently.

findings.title: The `(rule_id,)` enabled-set substitution in `project_suppressions` is unpinned
findings.why_it_matters: The project phase re-derives acceptance from a different `enabled_rules` argument than the file phase passes (`(rule_id,)` instead of the per-file `file_enabled_rules`). The two agree today because the only enabled-set-dependent check is the disabled-rule check. If `scan_pragmas` ever gains acceptance logic that depends on the enabled set (a rule-specific placement or language check), the phases drift. A pragma would be diagnosed in one phase and honoured in the other, with no signal. No test asserts that the project phase's accepted set for R matches the file phase's, and none crosses a per-file-ignore with a pragma naming a project rule.
findings.recommended: A: Add a parity test (unit equivalence over a few pragma samples, plus one per-file-ignore whole-run case in test_project_suppressions.py).
findings.chosen: A: Add a parity test (unit equivalence over a few pragma samples, plus one per-file-ignore whole-run case in test_project_suppressions.py).

findings.title: `Occurrence`, `PythonSources`, by-file grouping and `id()` claims answer one yes/no question
findings.why_it_matters: `pipeline.py` grew about 90 lines to answer "is this location claimed?". To trace why a finding was dropped, a reader crosses `expand_candidates`, `Occurrence`, `visible_occurrences`' group-by-path, the index list returned by `project_suppressions`, the mapping of indexes to `id()`s, the filter, and a count by subtraction. The `id()` set exists only because grouping loses the link between a returned index and its occurrence, and `Occurrence` compares by value (the code comment says so). `PythonSources` is a class that wraps one dict. This is a shape problem, paid on every read, and #39 and #61 will edit this path.
findings.recommended: A: Replace the grouping with a per-location predicate. `suppressions.claims_for(source, rule_id)` runs `scan_pragmas` once and returns `line -> bool` (`ignore_file or owner key in accepted owners`). `run_project_phase` keeps a parse memo by path and a predicate memo by `(rule_id, path)`. `expand_candidates` drops claimed locations as it builds findings and counts them. Delete `Occurrence`, `PythonSources`, the `id()` set and the subtraction.
findings.chosen: A: Replace the grouping with a per-location predicate. `suppressions.claims_for(source, rule_id)` runs `scan_pragmas` once and returns `line -> bool` (`ignore_file or owner key in accepted owners`). `run_project_phase` keeps a parse memo by path and a predicate memo by `(rule_id, path)`. `expand_candidates` drops claimed locations as it builds findings and counts them. Delete `Occurrence`, `PythonSources`, the `id()` set and the subtraction.

findings.title: The cache round-trips `related`, a field file-rule findings cannot have
findings.why_it_matters: The cache holds only file-phase results. Every cached `Finding` comes from `suppressions._public(candidate)`, and `CandidateFinding` has no `related` field (analysis.py:32-41), so the types guarantee `related == ()`. The Build call guards against "the day one doesn't". For that, `_finding_from_payload` gained a pop, an isinstance check and a nested `RelatedLocation(**_require_text(item, ("path",)))` rebuild that validates only `path`. A missing key now makes every entry "corrupted", and test_cache.py changed in three places. The guard isn't even safe: `_finding_to_payload` strips the finding's own `path` because the cache is content-keyed and the caller re-attaches it, but `related[*].path` round-trips verbatim. A future file rule with `related` would get stale paths after a file move, and the new test pins a foreign path's round trip (contract-caller).
findings.recommended: A: Drop `related` from the cache payload. `_finding_to_payload` deletes it alongside `path`, and `_finding_from_payload` goes back to master's form, so `related` defaults to `()`. Revert the test_cache.py round-trip of a foreign `RelatedLocation`. Amend Build call 4 to match.
findings.chosen: A: Drop `related` from the cache payload. `_finding_to_payload` deletes it alongside `path`, and `_finding_from_payload` goes back to master's form, so `related` defaults to `()`. Revert the test_cache.py round-trip of a foreign `RelatedLocation`. Amend Build call 4 to match.

findings.title: The occurrence-owner lookup lacks pins for except clauses and classes
findings.why_it_matters: The parametrized pins in test_project_suppressions.py cover only the D5 cases that use `def`. D5's own pin says "`def` or `class`", but no test uses a decorated `class`, and no test has a pragma on a `class` line. Nothing pins an occurrence on an `except` header line, where the Build call shares `refine_to_handler` between the two lookups so that they "can't drift". That sharing is the only protection. A later edit to `innermost_owner`'s key or to the decorated span could desync pragma owners from occurrence owners with no failing test. That's the "silently matches nothing" failure D5 was written to prevent.
findings.chosen: Add `pytest.param` rows (with sample sources) to `test_a_statement_pragma_claims_an_occurrence_through_its_owner` in tests/integration/test_project_suppressions.py:

findings.title: The PR description must carry the `BREAKING CHANGE:` footer
findings.why_it_matters: b6a0140 is `feat!:` with no footer. The squash commit's body is the PR description, so a footer that exists only in a branch commit is dropped (.claude/rules/changelog-quality.md). Without one, release-please publishes a breaking release with no note telling consumers that `schema_version == 2` checks now fail. The key added alongside the bump is additive, so the bump itself is what breaks a version-gated consumer.
findings.chosen: No file edit now. When creating the PR, end the description (after the attribution lines) with one footer:

findings.title: The ledger says `occurrence_owner` leaves `statement_owner_for_line` unchanged, but the build refactored it
findings.why_it_matters: The ledger's New homes line says `occurrence_owner` sits beside `statement_owner_for_line`, "which it doesn't change". D5's table rejected option B partly for "risk of change through the shared function". The build now ends `statement_owner_for_line` with `innermost_owner(...)`, which delegates to `refine_to_handler`, and the occurrence lookup shares both. The behaviour is equivalent (all three critics checked), and the sharing is the better design, since both lookups must agree on handler keys. Build call 3 records it. But the Summary line now contradicts Build call 3, and a reader of the ratified ledger is told the file-rule lookup is isolated when a tie-break edit in `innermost_owner` now changes file-rule ownership and HSL103 keys.
findings.recommended: A: In design.md's New homes, replace "which it doesn't change" with "sharing its innermost-statement choice and except-clause refinement (`innermost_owner`, `refine_to_handler`); file-rule behaviour is unchanged".
findings.chosen: A: In design.md's New homes, replace "which it doesn't change" with "sharing its innermost-statement choice and except-clause refinement (`innermost_owner`, `refine_to_handler`); file-rule behaviour is unchanged".

findings.title: The docs give a stale reason why project-rule pragmas are never reported as unused
findings.why_it_matters: docs/suppressions.md, which this change edited, says a pragma naming a project rule "is never reported as unused, because the rule's findings don't exist yet when the file is checked". The new CLAUDE.md gotcha says the same thing. That reason is now misleading. The project phase does resolve these pragmas against the rule's findings, so a reader concludes an unused verdict is impossible when it was actually declined: spec 010 D9 dropped it, following Pylint's exclusion of `duplicate-code` from useless-suppression. The user-facing consequence is real but accepted scope: a stale `ignore[HSL1xx]` stays forever with no report. The `_collect_claims` docstring is accurate for the file phase and can stay.
findings.recommended: A: Rewrite the reason in docs/suppressions.md and in the CLAUDE.md gotcha: a pragma naming a project rule is never reported as unused, by design (spec 010 D9). Finding stale ones would mean re-reading every file with such a pragma after the rule runs, and Pylint likewise excludes `duplicate-code` from unused-suppression checks.
findings.chosen: A: Rewrite the reason in docs/suppressions.md and in the CLAUDE.md gotcha: a pragma naming a project rule is never reported as unused, by design (spec 010 D9). Finding stale ones would mean re-reading every file with such a pragma after the rule runs, and Pylint likewise excludes `duplicate-code` from unused-suppression checks.

findings.title: A pragma-resolution crash is reported as the rule's `rule-run` failure
findings.why_it_matters: Resolution runs inside the rule's `try`, as ledger step 5 and the Posture require. A bug in `occurrence_owner` or `scan_pragmas`, triggered by one odd file, reports `internal_error("project", "rule-run", rule_id=...)`, stops the phase, and points triage at the rule rather than at pragma resolution. Without `--debug` there's no traceback and no file name. The fail-loud posture is right. Only the label misdirects.
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation: a pragma-resolution crash is reported as that rule's `rule-run` internal error, and `--debug` shows where it came from.
findings.chosen: B: Accept as a known limitation: a pragma-resolution crash is reported as that rule's `rule-run` internal error, and `--debug` shows where it came from.

findings.title: The project phase keeps every parsed tree until it ends
findings.why_it_matters: Audience assumption: a large repository where a rule's clusters span thousands of Python files. `PythonSources.parsed` holds a `PythonSource` (tree, tokens, text) for every Python file with at least one finding until the phase returns. `scan_pragmas` also re-runs per rule per file. For a personal tool this is negligible. It matters only if #39 reports findings across vendored or generated trees, and per-file-ignores are the stated escape hatch.
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation: the project phase holds one parsed tree per Python file with a finding until the phase ends. Revisit when #39 lands if memory shows up.
findings.chosen: B: Accept as a known limitation: the project phase holds one parsed tree per Python file with a finding until the phase ends. Revisit when #39 lands if memory shows up.

findings.title: A trailing pragma on a decorator line inside a class silently owns the class
findings.why_it_matters: Audience assumption: a many-contributor codebase with long-lived project rules. As D5 ratified, a trailing `ignore` on a method's decorator line keeps its file-rule owner, which is the enclosing `ClassDef`. The pragma is accepted (it's not "misplaced", unlike at module level). It doesn't claim the decorated method's occurrence (pinned by `decorator-line-pragma-in-class-misses-the-def`). It does silently claim any occurrence whose `occurrence_owner` is the class itself: one starting on the `class` line, or on a blank or comment line directly in the class body. The user wrote it beside a decorator, and it neither hides that duplicate nor gets reported, and spec 010 D9 means it's never called unused either.
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation: a trailing pragma on a method's decorator line is owned by the enclosing class and can claim class-owned occurrences, unreported.
findings.chosen: B: Accept as a known limitation: a trailing pragma on a method's decorator line is owned by the enclosing class and can claim class-owned occurrences, unreported.

findings.title: `summary.suppressed_count` now includes project-phase occurrences and is undocumented
findings.why_it_matters: Audience assumption: external JSON consumers who read the summary. The maintainer is the only known user. `suppressed_count` now sums suppressed file-phase findings and suppressed project-phase occurrences. Each occurrence would have been a finding, so the unit is still "suppressed findings". No doc defines the field, and that gap predates this change.
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation: `suppressed_count` has no written definition.
findings.chosen: B: Accept as a known limitation: `suppressed_count` has no written definition.

findings.title: Same-location findings sort by rule output order, and the text `(also at ...)` suffix has no stable delimiter
findings.why_it_matters: Audience assumption: parsers of text output, at larger scale. `ScanResult.to_dict` sorts findings by `(path, line, column, rule_id, message)`. Two findings with the same location and message but different `related` (one span in two candidates of one rule) keep input order. That's deterministic only while the rule's output order is. In text, `(also at ...)` follows a free-text message, so a message ending in a parenthetical, or a path containing `, `, is ambiguous. README says text output is for people.
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation: findings at the same location with the same message keep the rule's output order, and text output's `(also at ...)` isn't machine-delimited.
findings.chosen: B: Accept as a known limitation: findings at the same location with the same message keep the rule's output order, and text output's `(also at ...)` isn't machine-delimited.
